lessons.title: Hard or Soft, Rough or Smooth?
objectives: Describe objects as hard/soft and rough/smooth
Name the material something is made of
explanation: Everything is made of a material. A spoon might be metal, a chair might be wood, a cup might be plastic or glass, and a shirt is fabric.
We can describe materials by how they feel. A stone is hard; a pillow is soft. Sandpaper is rough; a mirror is smooth.
Some materials bend, like a rubber band or paper. Some stretch, like a balloon. Some don't bend at all, like a brick.

lessons.title: Will It Keep Me Dry?
objectives: Test which materials are waterproof

explanation: Some materials let water through; others keep water out. Materials that keep water out are called waterproof. Plastic, rubber and foil are waterproof. Paper towels and cotton soak water up.
We choose materials for their job. An umbrella needs to be waterproof. A towel needs to soak up water. A window needs to be see-through.

lessons.title: Can You Pour It?
objectives: Sort materials into solids and liquids
Describe properties of solids and liquids
explanation: A solid keeps its own shape. A block stays a block whether it's in a box or on a table. You can hold a solid in your hand.
A liquid flows and can be poured. It takes the shape of whatever container it is in — a tall glass or a flat plate.
Some things are tricky: sand and sugar can be poured, but each tiny grain is a solid that keeps its shape!

make something flow out
something that holds things

examples: Milk takes the shape of the glass.
Ice is solid water; tap water is liquid.

objectives: Observe that heating melts some solids and cooling freezes liquids
Know that melting and freezing can be reversed
explanation: When some solids get warm, they melt and turn into liquids. Ice melts into water. Butter and chocolate melt in the sun.
When some liquids get very cold, they freeze into solids. Water in a freezer becomes ice.
Melting and freezing can go backwards and forwards: water → ice → water. We call this a reversible change.

lessons.title: Where Did the Puddle Go?
objectives: Describe the three states of matter
Explain evaporation and condensation
explanation: There are three common states of matter: solid, liquid and gas. A gas spreads out to fill any container. Air is a mixture of gases — you can't see it, but you can feel it as wind.
Evaporation is when a liquid turns into a gas. A puddle disappears on a sunny day because the water evaporates into water vapour in the air. Heat makes it happen faster.
Condensation is the opposite: a gas cooling into a liquid. Water droplets form on a cold glass because water vapour in the air cools on it.

vocabulary.meaning: a state that spreads out to fill any space
liquid changing to gas
gas changing to liquid
water as a gas

examples: Wet clothes dry on a washing line by evaporation.
A bathroom mirror fogs up by condensation.

lessons.title: Where Did the Sugar Go?
objectives: Test which solids dissolve in water
Investigate what makes dissolving faster
explanation: When sugar is stirred into water, it seems to vanish. It has dissolved: it has broken into pieces too tiny to see and spread through the water. Taste it — the sweetness proves it's still there!
Materials that dissolve are soluble (sugar, salt). Materials that don't are insoluble (sand, chalk). The mixture of a dissolved solid in a liquid is called a solution.
Dissolving is faster in warm water and when stirred, and smaller pieces dissolve faster than big lumps.

context.text: Never taste unknown substances in experiments. Only taste kitchen ingredients like sugar or salt with an adult's permission.

vocabulary.meaning: mix completely into a liquid so you can't see it

lessons.title: The Separation Challenge
objectives: Choose a method to separate a mixture
Explain how each method uses a property of materials
explanation: A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined, so they can be separated using their properties.

Sieving separates by size (rice from small stones). Filtering separates insoluble solids from liquids (sand from water). Evaporating separates dissolved solids from water (salt from sea water). A magnet separates magnetic metals (iron filings from sand).
For a tricky mixture, use methods in order: e.g. sand, salt and iron — magnet first, then add water and filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to get salt.

vocabulary.meaning: substances mixed but not chemically joined
separate an insoluble solid from a liquid
separate by size
remove liquid by turning it into gas

examples: Salt pans on India's coasts evaporate sea water to collect salt.

units.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes

lessons.title: Can We Undo It?
objectives: Classify changes as reversible or irreversible
Recognise signs that a new substance has formed
explanation: Reversible changes can be undone: melting, freezing, dissolving and evaporating. No new substance is made.
Irreversible changes make new substances and can't easily be undone: cooking an egg, baking a cake, burning wood, and iron rusting.
Signs of a chemical (irreversible) change include: a new colour, gas bubbles, a smell, light or heat given off, or a new solid forming.

vocabulary.meaning: a change that can be undone
a change that makes new substances and cannot easily be undone
a new substance formed when iron reacts with water and oxygen
a change that makes a new substance

examples: Burning a candle: wax reacts to make gases (irreversible), though melting wax is reversible.
Mixing vinegar and baking soda makes bubbles of carbon dioxide gas.

story.title: The Uncooked Egg Wish

activities.prompt: Reversible or irreversible?

lessons.title: Dancing Particles
objectives: Use the particle model to explain properties of solids, liquids and gases
Explain diffusion
prerequisites: Knows three states of matter and changes of state
explanation: All matter is made of tiny particles far too small to see. In a solid, particles are packed closely in a fixed pattern and vibrate in place — so solids keep their shape.
In a liquid, particles are close but can slide past each other — so liquids flow. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions — so gases spread out.

Heating gives particles more energy, so they move faster. That's why heating melts solids and evaporates liquids. Diffusion — like a smell spreading through a room — happens because particles move and mix.

vocabulary.meaning: a tiny piece of matter
particles spreading from crowded to less crowded areas
move back and forth on the spot
the idea that particles are always moving

examples: Smell of agarbatti spreading through a room: diffusion.

story.title: The Spreading Smell

lessons.title: The Periodic Table
objectives: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures
Find basic information on the periodic table
explanation: An element is a substance made of only one type of atom — like oxygen (O), iron (Fe) or gold (Au). About 118 elements are known, arranged in the periodic table.

A compound is made when atoms of different elements chemically join, like water (H₂O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen) or carbon dioxide (CO₂). Compounds have different properties from their elements: sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine a poisonous gas, but together they make table salt (NaCl).
The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number. Columns (groups) contain elements with similar properties; metals are on the left and middle, non-metals on the right.

context.text: Dmitri Mendeleev published an early periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements whose properties he predicted — several were later discovered.

vocabulary.meaning: the smallest particle of an element
a substance of one type of atom
two or more elements chemically joined
symbols showing the atoms in a compound

examples: O₂: oxygen gas (an element, two atoms joined).
Air is a mixture; water is a compound.

story.title: Mendeleev's Card Game
story.text: The chemist Dmitri Mendeleev wrote each known element on a card with its properties and arranged them like a game of patience. He noticed repeating patterns — and boldly left gaps, predicting elements no one had found. When gallium and germanium were discovered, they fitted his predictions.

lessons.title: Balancing Equations
objectives: Write word and symbol equations
Balance equations using conservation of mass
explanation: In a chemical reaction, reactants rearrange into products. Atoms are not created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same — the law of conservation of mass.
Word equation: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Symbol equation: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
To balance, count atoms of each element on both sides and adjust the large numbers in front (coefficients), never the small subscripts. Here: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O on each side.

context.text: Antoine Lavoisier's careful weighing experiments in the 1770s–1780s established conservation of mass in chemical reactions.

vocabulary.meaning: a starting substance in a reaction
a substance formed
number in front of a formula showing how many units
total mass is unchanged in a reaction

examples: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

story.title: Lavoisier's Scales
story.text: In the 1770s, Antoine Lavoisier sealed substances in glass vessels and weighed them before and after heating. Even when substances changed completely, the sealed total mass stayed the same. Matter was rearranging, not appearing or vanishing — a turning point for chemistry.

activities.prompt: Balance: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. Correct:

thinking: Why does a burning candle seem to lose mass if mass is conserved?

speaking: Teach someone to balance CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O step by step.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and the pH Scale
objectives: Use indicators and the pH scale
Explain neutralisation and factors affecting reaction rate
explanation: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Acids have pH below 7 (lemon juice ≈ 2), neutral substances pH 7 (pure water), and bases/alkalis above 7 (soap, baking soda solution).

Indicators change colour with pH. Red cabbage juice turns red/pink in acids and green/yellow in strong alkalis. Acid + base → salt + water: this is neutralisation, used in antacid tablets and treating acidic soils.
Reaction rates increase with higher temperature, higher concentration, larger surface area (powder vs lump) and catalysts — because particles collide more often or with more energy.

vocabulary.meaning: a substance with pH below 7
a substance that neutralises acids (alkalis are soluble bases)
a substance that changes colour with pH
a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up

examples: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
Powdered sugar dissolves and reacts faster than a sugar cube due to greater surface area.
